catalog_quote: The Mara languages have previously been reported as accentual or “two type” languages with fairly reduced or non-existent lexical tonal contrasts (Bastin 2003). However, a closer look at the Mara languages shows that many have more than two lexical tonal contrasts and make use of melodic tones in their verbal systems. [...] The underlying contrast is between H and Ø (toneless) since only H tones are active in the tonal rules. There is at most one lexical H tone per morpheme with the exception of Kabwa double H pattern (see below). [...] In Kabwa, utterance-final Hs are deleted (see explanation following Table 8). [...] Kabwa has n+1 patterns, i.e. two for monosyllabic, three for bisyllabic and four for trisyllabic noun stems (cf. Table 8 and following explanation). [...] All six languages lack lexical tonal contrast in the verb stem. In Ikoma (12), Kabwa (13), and Simbiti (14), all verb stems in the Infinitive have a H on the first syllable of the macrostem [...] Kabwa assigns melodic Hs to the first syllable of the macrostem or to the whole macrostem.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kabwa is described as a tone language with a privative H vs toneless contrast, not as a stress language. Noun stems carry a lexical H in one of four lexically determined positions (final H, penult H, double H, antepenult H; Table 8), H spreads rightward in some contexts, and utterance-final H is deleted (so final-H and double-H nouns are all-low in isolation). Verb stems have no lexical tone; grammatical (melodic) H falls on the first syllable of the macrostem (infinitive: òkù-[ɾúmà 'to bite') or on the whole macrostem, some forms have H on the TAM prefix, and some forms are toneless. No word-stress rule is stated for Kabwa. The only stress remark anywhere is the Orthography Statement p. 8, which says a root long vowel in derived verbs 'is sometimes shortened in normal pronunciation, perhaps due to the stress placed on a later syllable' — an unanalysed hint that phonetic prominence falls late in the word (presumably the penult), not a rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Aunio et al. note that 'regular penultimate stress' exists only for some Zanaki speakers, possibly under Swahili influence, and weight-determined tone placement for Ngoreme; neither is said of Kabwa. Orthography Statement §2.3.1 (p. 15): only one tonal minimal pair found (omusimu 'arrow' vs 'season'), lexical tone judged to have low functional load and is not. §2.3.3 (p. 16): Remote Past has H on the verb root vs all-low General Present ([twaagúɾa] vs [twaaguɾa]).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tonal analysis based on the authors' field data (SIL Kabwa team); tones cited are phrase-medial forms because utterance-final H is deleted in Kabwa (isolation/citation forms neutralise final-H and double-H nouns). Nouns and infinitives/inflected verbs both covered.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Kabwa proper (ISO cwa, Guthrie/Maho JE405), Mara Region, Tanzania; the Orthography Statement (§1.3, p. 6) states Kabwa 'is perceived internally as having only one dialect' (Kiroba and Sweta, its closest relatives, belong to Suba-Simbiti [ssc], suba1254). Aunio et al. 2019 treat Kabwa as one of six Mara corpus languages; the Kabwa data come from the SIL Kabwa team (Walker, Robinson). The SIL OAI record dates the orthography statement 2012 (Walker, Meszaros, Robinson) but the document itself is the 'Approved Orthography Edition: December 2017' authored by Rebekah Overton and John B. Walker (Meszaros and Overton are evidently the same person).

tone_statements.citation: Walker, John B. 2013. Comparative tense and aspect in the Mara Bantu languages: towards a linguistic history. MA thesis, Trinity Western University. 308 pp.
tone_statements.quote: The P4 has a high-tone on the vowel of the root. This contrasts tonally with the PRS in Kabwa, which has all low tones (SM-aa-R-a). [fn 46] ... There is a high-tone that appears to surface on the penultimate mora for this form in Kabwa: [tʷaágʲa] ‘we went (before yesterday)’; [tʷaagúɾa] ‘we bought (before yesterday)’. [fn 61] ... Tone is generally not marked in the orthographies of the Mara languages other than a few isolated minimal pairs for grammatical tone in Ikoma ... When it is merely the tonal pattern differentiating one TAM formative from another, I make special note of the surface differences in prose. However, underlying tonal patterns cannot be ascertained until fuller descriptions of the verbal tone systems in these languages have been undertaken, which is beyond the scope of my research.
tone_statements.locator: also p. 89 (PDF 102), p. 147 fn 165 (PDF 160), Kabwa TA chart pp. 168-169 fns 182, 185 (PDF 181-182)
tone_statements.check: quotation from the author's open copy, read 2026-09-25; not yet verified by a second reading
tone_statements.summary: Tense/aspect thesis, not a prosodic description. It confirms that Kabwa uses tone grammatically: a High vs Low contrast distinguishes TA formatives (P4 far past SM-aa-Ŕ-a with a high tone on the root, surfacing on the penultimate mora, vs the all-low Vast Present SM-aa-R-a; Kabwa chart fns 182 and 185 repeat this). Only surface tone is noted, and only where it is the main differentiator of a minim

sources.note: Table 8 (tables draft p. 8) lists four Kabwa nominal tone classes with underlying tones: final H (òβù-sú 'nest', èŋ-gìgé 'locust'), penult H (òβú-sù 'face', èŋ-gégè 'tilapia'), double H (èŋ-gíhó 'kidney'), antepenult H (è-góɾòhè 'billy-goat'). Nothing on stress.
